h1: Building a project timeline for a brewpub from lease to launch
title: Brewpub Timeline: Lease to Launch | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build a brewpub project timeline from lease signing to opening night, with the licence path, fit out and brewing tests in the right order.
teaser: Most brewpub openings slip for the same reason: the licence and the fit out were planned as if they did not depend on each other.
standfirst: A brewpub has two critical paths running side by side: the paperwork and the building. This guide shows how to lay them out so that rent stops burning before the first pint does.
sections: The licence path sets the pace, not the builder

Founders usually plan around the fit out because it is visible. The quiet driver is the approvals chain. In most states the brewpub or microbrewery licence comes late in the sequence, after building approvals, a fire NOC, pollution board consent and a trade licence. Several of those need the finished layout or even the finished premises before an inspector will sign. Rules and timelines vary by state and change, so ask a licensing consultant to map the steps for your city before you sign anything.

The practical rule: draw the licence path first, then fit the construction plan around it. If the excise inspection needs installed vessels, the brewhouse has to arrive before the paperwork can finish. That single dependency decides half your schedule.
Count backwards from the rent-free period

Every week between lease signing and first sale is rent with no revenue against it. If your landlord grants a rent-free fit out period, that number becomes the frame for the whole plan. Our guide on negotiating a rent-free fit out period covers how to ask for it.

Work it as arithmetic. Suppose rent is R a month and the realistic gap to opening is nine months, of which three are rent free. You are funding six months of rent from capital before the bar takes a rupee. Put that figure in the project budget as its own line. Founders who hide it inside contingency find out in month seven that contingency was spent on stainless.

Every site differs, but the sequence below is the one we use as a starting skeleton:

  1. Site due diligence before signing: zoning, structural capacity, water, power, drainage and whether a brewpub is permitted at that address at all.
  2. Lease signed, architect and MEP consultant appointed, layout frozen.
  3. Brewhouse ordered the week the layout is frozen. Fabrication lead times run to months.
  4. Building and fire approvals filed on the frozen drawings.
  5. Civil work: drains, floor falls, structural strengthening, then services.
  6. Brewhouse delivery, installation and commissioning.
  7. Inspections and licence issue.
  8. Test brews, staff training, soft opening.

The step founders skip is the third. A layout that keeps changing means a vessel order that cannot be placed. Every redesign in month two shows up as a delay in month eight.
Leave room for beer to be beer

The licence arriving does not mean beer is ready. An ale takes around two to three weeks from brew day to a bright, carbonated pint. A clean lager needs four to six. If you want six taps on opening night, the first ales must go in about a month before and any lager six weeks or more before. The licence has to land before either. In most states you cannot brew legally before it does.

Plan at least two water-only runs through the brewhouse during commissioning, then a test batch you are prepared to pour down the drain. The first real brew on a new system rarely hits its numbers. Mash efficiency, boil-off and chiller performance all need a day or two of measured tuning.
A soft opening belongs inside the schedule

Put two weeks of soft opening on the plan as real tasks, not as a hopeful gap before launch. Invite friends, neighbours and the people who helped with the build. Run the kitchen at half the menu. Pour four beers, not eight. Every problem you find in that fortnight (a slow POS, a tap that pours foam, a dishwasher on the wrong circuit) is one the paying public never sees.

Staff need the same runway. Bar teams should taste every beer and practise pouring before the doors open. Hire them three to four weeks before opening and budget their wages for that period. It is cheaper than a first review that mentions flat beer and a confused server.
Track the plan where everyone can see it

A brewpub project has a landlord, an architect, a fabricator, a kitchen consultant, a licensing adviser and a founder who is usually also the finance team. A single Gantt chart in a shared spreadsheet works better than six people's memory. List each task with its owner, its earliest start, its dependency and a date it must finish by to protect opening.

Mark the critical path in a different colour. Review it every Monday. When a task slips, the question is never only how late it is. The question is whether it sits on the critical path. A two week delay on bar stools is noise. A two week delay on the fire NOC is two weeks of rent.

In our work the same three failures repeat. The first is power: a sanctioned load that cannot carry the brewhouse, the kitchen and the glycol chiller at once, discovered after the walls are closed. The second is drainage that was never designed for hot caustic and spent grain. The third is the opening date announced on social media before the licence was in hand.

None of these is a brewing problem. They are planning problems, which is why they can be fixed on paper at almost no cost if somebody looks early. The Brewery Business Management course walks through costing, phasing and the order of approvals in a format you can reuse for your own site.
faqs: How long does it take to open a brewpub in India?
It depends on the state, the site and how quickly approvals move. Plan the licence path first with a consultant, then build the fit out around it. Allow time for test brews after the licence arrives.
When should I order the brewhouse?
As soon as the layout is frozen. Fabrication takes months. Some excise inspections need installed vessels before the licence is issued.
Can I brew before the licence is issued?
In most states no. Check the current rules for your state with a licensing adviser before planning any test brews.
